One immediate emergency must not cause the crew to forget an unrelated unresolved exposure boundary.

### Additional exposure decisions: radiation, infection, and coatings
TENORM means naturally occurring radioactive material whose concentration or accessibility has been increased by human activity. Oil and gas production can concentrate radionuclides in scale and sludge. External radiation and inhaling or ingesting contaminated particles are different exposure routes; long-term radiation exposure can increase cancer risk. Ordinary PPE does not shield every form of penetrating radiation. Keep tagged material undisturbed, prevent dust generation and hand-to-mouth transfer, and obtain specialist survey and disposal instructions. Do not assume all produced equipment is radioactive, or that an absence of a tag establishes that it is clean.

Infectious disease prevention also concerns person-to-person spread, not only bites and contaminated waste. Follow the employer's illness-reporting, cleaning, ventilation, and exposure arrangements. Wash hands before eating and after contamination; use the designated cleaning products as instructed. Cover coughs and avoid sharing contaminated personal items. If ill, seek guidance before joining close-contact work or shared transport. Do not conceal symptoms to avoid delaying a crew, and do not diagnose or exclude coworkers based on rumor. The particular infection and workplace determine additional precautions; bloodborne controls do not automatically control airborne transmission.

Welding stainless steel or disturbing some chromium-containing coatings can create hexavalent chromium exposure. Its serious effects include respiratory disease and cancer; skin or eye contact can also cause harm. Identify the material and process, obtain the required exposure assessment and ventilation or other controls, and follow respiratory and hygiene arrangements when applicable. Do not infer that an ordinary dust mask or outdoor location makes fume exposure safe. General-industry 1910.1026 and construction 1926.1126 have distinct applicability and conditional medical requirements.

For a lift remaining after elimination and handling-aid review, check the destination and clear the route before grasping the load. Test whether you can handle it without strain; do not jerk an unexpectedly heavy object. Bring the load close, establish balanced footing, bend through hips and knees as appropriate, and rise smoothly without twisting. Turn by moving your feet and set the load down with controlled hands and a clear landing place. Stop if grip, visibility, or footing is inadequate. Tool ergonomics also requires neutral wrist positions, suitable handle size, supported work height, reduced sustained grip, and management of repetition and vibration. Rotate tasks only as part of a real exposure-reduction plan, not to distribute an excessive hazard to more people.

lessons.title: Journey management, driving, and mobile-equipment interfaces
lessons.body:
## Learning objectives
- Plan a journey around driver fitness, vehicle condition, route, weather, and communication.
- Explain pedestrian separation, spotting, backing, and load-interface controls.
- Distinguish driving permission from equipment-specific operator qualification.
- Work through fatigue and delivery scenarios using stop-and-reassess decisions.

### Treat transportation as part of the job
A trip between facilities can expose a worker to more risk than the task at the destination. Rural roads may combine darkness, dust, wildlife, narrow bridges, school traffic, heavy trucks, and drivers unfamiliar with the route. On a location, short vehicle movements can create fatal crushing hazards. A good journey plan addresses the driver, vehicle, route, load, timing, and receiving location together. It also establishes what to do when the plan becomes unsafe. Meeting a delivery time does not justify continuing with failed brakes, inadequate visibility, or fatigue.

Before departure, confirm the trip is necessary and choose the approved vehicle and route. Check weather, flooding, road closures, overhead clearance, surface conditions, available fuel or charging, and safe stopping places. Obtain precise access instructions and a destination contact; navigation software can direct a vehicle through a restricted entrance or unsuitable road. Know the check-in process and how an overdue journey will be escalated. Where communication coverage is poor, arrange an approved alternative. A journey plan is a working agreement, not permission to use a phone while driving.


### Fitness and vehicle readiness
Fatigue reduces attention, reaction, and judgment. Extended shifts, overnight work, long commutes, poor sleep, medications, and illness can combine. Warning signs include repeated yawning, wandering thoughts, missed turns, lane drift, and difficulty recalling the last miles. Do not wait for a near collision. Stop in a safe place and notify the designated contact to arrange rest, a relief driver, or another transport option. Loud music, an open window, and caffeine do not replace adequate sleep. Do not use an unsafe shoulder or park in an operating equipment route just to meet a check-in time.

Disclose work-relevant impairment through the employer's confidential fitness process. Prescription or nonprescription medicine may affect driving even when legally obtained. Do not diagnose yourself from a package label alone when symptoms or the task raise doubt; seek appropriate guidance. Alcohol, recreational drugs, and medication misuse are incompatible with safe operation. Employer rules and applicable transportation regulations may impose additional duties. This lesson does not invent a universal hours-of-service limit or establish commercial-driver qualification.

Inspect the vehicle using the applicable checklist: tires, lights, windows, mirrors, seat belts, fluid leaks, steering, brakes, and required emergency equipment. Walk around before moving and look beneath or behind where someone or something could be hidden. Confirm occupants have suitable seats and restraints. Secure tools and cargo so they cannot become projectiles during braking. A warning light, damaged restraint, or unsecured heavy item requires evaluation and correction; reporting it after the trip does not protect the current occupants. Remove an unsafe vehicle from service through the designated process.


### Driving with changing conditions
Wear the seat belt before movement and require passengers to do the same. Set navigation and communications before departure. Park safely before reading or composing messages; a dispatch request does not remove distraction. Adjust speed and following distance to visibility, traction, load, and stopping space. The posted limit is not a promise that it is safe in fog, dust, ice, or heavy rain. Leave room for a loaded vehicle's greater stopping demands and changing center of gravity. Avoid sudden steering and braking.

Do not drive through water where depth, current, road support, or escape is uncertain. Turn around safely and report the route problem. On lease roads, expect vehicles at blind curves and crests; follow designated right-of-way and radio arrangements without assuming the other driver heard you. Approach railroad crossings under the vehicle's applicable procedure and never stop on tracks. Plan clearance for trailers and long loads. If visibility collapses, find a safe place outside traffic and equipment paths rather than following taillights into an unknown hazard.

Parking is a task requiring controls. Use designated spaces away from well-control equipment, evacuation paths, fire equipment, and suspended-load areas. Follow the location's engine, ignition-source, and vehicle-orientation rules. Apply parking brakes and use required stabilization or wheel chocks for the specific operation. Exit facing the vehicle with stable handholds and footing; jumping from a cab can turn an otherwise safe journey into an injury. Check the walking route before stepping into traffic.


### Pedestrians and mobile equipment
Separate people and machines with planned lanes, barriers, controlled crossings, speed management, and clear communication. A high-visibility vest improves recognition but does not stop a truck. Stay out of blind spots, articulation areas, counterweight swing zones, and the space between a moving vehicle and a fixed object. Make positive contact with the operator through the agreed system before approaching. Eye contact alone may be impossible through glare, tinted windows, or distance; do not interpret a glance as permission to enter.

Avoid backing where layout can provide forward travel. When backing is necessary, use the site procedure and a designated trained spotter when required. Agree signals, travel route, safe spotter position, and a stop signal before movement. The spotter must remain visible and outside the vehicle's path with an escape route. If visual or communication contact is lost, the operator stops. Cameras, alarms, and sensors supplement the plan; they do not prove the path is clear. Anyone identifying an immediate danger should use the established stop signal.

Forklifts, loaders, telehandlers, cranes, and other mobile machines have different operating limits. A road driver's license or a previous job title does not authorize their use. Powered industrial truck operation under 1910.178 requires appropriate training and evaluation, including practical elements, and employer certification. Equipment type, attachments, terrain, and workplace conditions matter. Construction equipment may be subject to 1926 provisions such as 1926.602. This online lesson cannot provide the practical evaluation, license, or task authorization.


### Loading and unloading interfaces
A load can shift when restraints are released. Before unloading, the driver and receiving crew establish who controls movement, the exclusion zone, stable ground, capacity, load condition, and the sequence. Look for leaning cargo, damaged packaging, stressed straps, and stored energy. Do not stand where falling pipe, rolling material, a released strap, or moving forks could strike. Use suitable equipment and designated methods for restraints; never cut or release a suspect restraint from its line of fire.

Keep people away from suspended or elevated loads. Do not walk beneath raised forks, ride on a load, or use a pallet as an improvised personnel platform. Do not use your hands or body to steady material where you can be trapped. Rigging, signaling, and lifting qualifications must match the task. If a load has shifted, stop and have the unloading plan revised by qualified personnel. A convenient vacant area is unsuitable if its surface cannot support the equipment or it blocks emergency access.


### Worked scenario: fatigued return trip
After an extended repair, Priya is scheduled to drive a crew ninety minutes back to the yard. She notices repeated yawning before leaving and realizes she slept poorly before the shift. A coworker says the truck has lane assistance and offers coffee. Priya reports she is not fit for the journey and keeps the vehicle parked. The supervisor checks whether a rested authorized driver is available and arranges safe transport and recovery time rather than moving the same fatigue problem to another tired crew member.

The departure time, replacement arrangement, and changed check-in are communicated to the receiving contact. Nobody is instructed to make up time by speeding. The supervisor later reviews why the shift and travel plan produced an unsafe return. This is a successful intervention even though no collision occurred. Fatigue reporting supplied the information needed to change the work arrangement before an incident.


### Worked scenario: pipe delivery at a crowded pad
A delivery driver arrives where the normal unloading lane is blocked by a service truck. A loader operator offers to back across a pedestrian route and unload beside a drainage edge. The receiver stops the movement. They review ground support, identify the pedestrian conflict, clear the proper lane, and establish a barrier and crossing control. The driver remains in the agreed safe location while an authorized operator prepares the approved unloading area.

During inspection, one pipe bundle appears to lean against a restraint. The crew does not simply release it because the loader is waiting. Qualified personnel revise the restraint-removal and stabilization sequence and keep workers out of the potential roll path. A trained spotter is positioned with visibility and escape; when dust hides that spotter, the operator stops until contact is restored. After unloading, the driver checks the empty vehicle and confirms the route is clear before departure. The outcome relies on coordination at each interface, not on one person's confidence.

lessons.title: Tools, guarding, PPE, and walking-working surfaces
lessons.body:
## Learning objectives
- Inspect tools and PPE for task suitability, condition, and limitations.
- Recognize guarding, energy-control, and entanglement boundaries.
- Control housekeeping and walking-surface hazards before exposure.
- Apply defect reporting and stop-work decisions in worked situations.

### Select the method before picking up the tool
An ordinary hand tool can become a high-energy hazard when it slips, breaks, or contacts energized equipment. A powered tool adds rotation, flying material, electricity, pressure, heat, and noise. Before work, confirm what the task requires, what energy or material is present, and whether you are authorized to perform it. Choose the right tool, accessory, capacity, and work position. If the proposed method requires a missing guard, an improvised extension, or placing a hand in a pinch point, the method needs to change before work begins.

Read and follow manufacturer instructions together with the employer's task procedure. Check the work area for flammable atmosphere, combustible material, nearby people, overhead work, and hidden services. A grinder can create an ignition source even when the job is called cold maintenance. A battery-powered device can still create sparks and stored-energy hazards. Tools used in classified areas must have the required suitability; an ordinary label or your own tape does not make a tool approved. Obtain the applicable authorization rather than assuming portability means unrestricted use.


### Inspect and control defects
Inspect hand tools for cracked handles, loose heads, mushroomed striking surfaces, damaged grips, worn jaws, and incorrect size. Use a wrench that fits; do not add a pipe to obtain more leverage unless the equipment and procedure specifically permit it. Do not strike a tool that is not designed for striking. Cut away from the body with a suitable controlled blade and secure the work. Keep fingers outside the path that a slipping blade or wrench would travel. Never use a screwdriver as a substitute chisel or pry bar just because it fits a gap.

For power tools, inspect housings, switches, cords, plugs, battery packs, guards, and accessories before use. Match accessories to the manufacturer's specifications, including size and speed rating. A damaged abrasive wheel or incompatible attachment can fail violently. Check pneumatic hoses, fittings, and retention devices; secure connections using the specified system. Do not carry a tool by its hose or cord. Protect leads and hoses from sharp edges, traffic, heat, and pinch points. Use the electrical protection required for the environment and applicable rules.

When a defect affects safety, stop using the equipment and prevent inadvertent reuse. Tag and segregate it through the site's process, tell the responsible person, and obtain a suitable replacement. A tag without physical control may leave the item available to the next shift. Tape over damaged insulation is not an authorized repair by itself. Do not bypass an interlock to test whether the machine still works. Repairs and return to service require authorized personnel and the applicable inspection. Record the observed defect accurately rather than declaring an untested cause.


### Guarding and energy control
Machine guards separate people from points of operation, rotating parts, nip points, belts, chains, and flying material. A guard must protect without introducing a new hazard. Know the safe operating position and keep hands outside hazardous areas. Gloves, loose sleeves, jewelry, and unsecured long hair can be drawn into rotation; follow the task's entanglement controls. A glove may protect against a sharp edge while being unsuitable near rotating machinery. PPE selection must consider both hazards rather than treating more equipment as automatically safer.

An emergency stop is not the same as energy isolation. A machine can restart, coast, fall, release pressure, or move from stored energy after its normal switch is turned off. Clearing jams, changing certain components, cleaning inside guards, or servicing may require the employer's hazardous-energy-control procedure. Only authorized workers perform the isolation and verification for their role. Do not reach through or remove a guard because a machine appears idle. If your role is affected employee, recognize the boundary and contact the authorized person rather than removing another worker's lock.

General-industry guarding provisions include 1910.212 and power-tool rules such as 1910.243. Construction has different provisions including 1926.300. The applicable rule depends on the activity and equipment; not every oilfield task is construction. This lesson provides recognition and decision skills, not authorization to service equipment, perform electrical work, or certify guards. Ask for the task-specific demonstration before using unfamiliar equipment and stop if instructions conflict with the physical arrangement.


### PPE as a fitted, maintained barrier
The hazard assessment determines the needed eye, face, head, hand, foot, body, hearing, and respiratory protection. Select the specified type and size and inspect it before use. Safety glasses and a face shield have different functions; a shield normally supplements the required primary eye protection for flying-particle tasks. Chemical splash, grinding fragments, arc hazards, and optical radiation need different protective selections. Ordinary sunglasses do not substitute for the required eye protection. Do not enter a task relying on an unidentified lens or damaged shell.

Inspect straps, soles, lenses, seams, fasteners, and contamination. A hard hat with damage or unauthorized alterations needs evaluation under the manufacturer's requirements. Chemical-resistant gloves must match the substance and anticipated contact, not simply be thick. Replace damaged PPE through the designated process and store it away from damaging sunlight, chemicals, and heat. Share reusable items only under the approved cleaning and fit arrangements. PPE that prevents a reliable grip or impairs communication requires reassessment, not silent adaptation.

Required respirator use ordinarily brings program requirements such as selection, medical evaluation, fit testing for tight-fitting models, training, and maintenance under 1910.134. A seal check at each use is not a substitute for fit testing. Facial hair or other interference can defeat the seal. Do not borrow a respirator and assume it is suitable. Fall-protection equipment likewise requires task-specific selection, inspection, anchorage, rescue planning, and practical training beyond this lesson. Completion here does not prove any hands-on competency.


### Housekeeping and walking-working surfaces
Keep work areas orderly as the task progresses. Store materials so they cannot fall, roll, obstruct access, or block fire and emergency equipment. Control sharp waste and protrusions; arrange disposal rather than leaving scraps for the end of a shift. Route hoses and cords away from walking paths or use approved protection and crossings. A housekeeping problem often indicates poor work layout, not simply an untidy worker. Plan staging areas and removal intervals so cleanliness can be maintained without entering operating equipment zones.

Inspect the route for oil, mud, ice, loose gravel, holes, changes in elevation, damaged grating, unsupported covers, and inadequate lighting. Stop and protect an unsafe route until it is repaired or a safe alternative established. Do not place an unmarked scrap plate over an opening and assume it is a suitable cover. Report missing rails and damaged stairs. Use handrails, keep sight of the route, and carry items so you can maintain balance. Suitable footwear helps but does not make a contaminated surface safe.

Choose an appropriate ladder or access system instead of a bucket, pallet, or equipment guard. Inspect ladders and set them up under their instructions and the applicable procedure. Maintain secure contact and do not overreach sideways or carry a load that defeats safe climbing. Elevated work requires the relevant fall-protection controls; do not infer that a short task is exempt. A mobile access platform has operator and equipment requirements separate from ladder use. Wet boots, gloves, and poor lighting can combine with an otherwise acceptable access method to create a fall.


### Worked scenario: a grinder and a tight deadline
A technician finds the correct-size grinder has a cracked guard. Another grinder has an intact guard but an accessory of uncertain rating. The crew is waiting to fit a replacement bracket. The technician rejects both as currently presented, tags and separates the damaged tool, and asks for an approved combination. The supervisor confirms the work authorization, nearby combustibles, suitable accessory, secure workholding, and eye, face, hearing, and other specified protection.

Before starting, they notice the power lead would cross a busy walkway. They reroute and protect it rather than telling pedestrians to step over it. The authorized technician completes the work using the intact guard and safe operating position. The damaged grinder remains out of service for repair. A replacement tool alone would not have corrected the trip hazard or ignition-source question, so the whole setup needed review.


### Worked scenario: a stopped conveyor and oily access
At a service yard, Dana sees a small jam on a conveyor and a puddle at its access stair. A coworker offers to hold the stop button while Dana removes the obstruction. Dana refuses to reach inside because stopping does not establish isolation. She prevents access to the affected area and contacts the authorized maintenance worker. The worker follows the specific energy-control procedure, including stored-energy checks and verification before exposure.

Separately, the supervisor arranges safe leak control and cleanup and checks whether the stair surface needs repair. Dana does not spread absorbent into a moving mechanism or step through the puddle to reach a better handhold. The crew records both hazards and verifies the guard, work area, and access are restored before authorized restart. Treating the jam and the walking route as separate controls prevents one correction from concealing another unresolved risk.

lessons.title: Emergency action, first aid, fire, and spill boundaries
lessons.body:
## Learning objectives
- Use the site emergency plan to alarm, evacuate, account, and communicate.
- Distinguish trained first aid from unsafe rescue and unqualified medical treatment.
- Recognize bloodborne-exposure precautions and prompt reporting.
- Determine when fire or spill conditions require withdrawal and specialist response.

### Learn the plan before an alarm
An emergency is a poor time to discover the address, radio channel, or assembly location. At orientation, learn how the site reports emergencies, what alarms mean, where primary and alternate exits lead, and how accountability works. Identify who contacts public responders and who meets them at a safe access point. Know the location's name, entrance, coordinates or address, and any access restrictions. A remote pad may need a gate opened and a guide positioned far from the hazard; provide this information through the plan rather than assuming a dispatcher recognizes the lease name.

The emergency action plan identifies evacuation arrangements and any designated roles such as shutdown, rescue, medical response, or accounting for personnel. Do not assign yourself a special role during an incident. General-industry 1910.38 applies when another standard requires an emergency action plan; construction includes 1926.35. Not every provision applies identically to every site. Regardless of classification, understand the actual site instructions before work. A plan on a wall is not sufficient if contract crews cannot recognize the alarm or find a safe route.


### Alarm, move, and account
When you discover an emergency, protect yourself first, alert others using the established signal, and notify the emergency contact. Give location, what happened, hazards observed, number of people affected if known, and a safe approach direction. Avoid unsupported claims such as declaring an atmosphere safe because nobody smells gas. Follow the evacuation or shelter instructions for the event. A gas release, lightning, severe weather, or security threat may require different protective actions. Do not automatically use the nearest enclosed room for every hazard.

Move by a safe route away from the hazard and follow the designated assembly process. Consider wind indicators and site instructions for releases, but do not cross a visible plume to reach a preferred muster sign. If the primary route is blocked, use the identified alternate and report your location. Leave possessions behind when retrieving them delays escape. Do not drive a vehicle through a release or bring an ignition source into a suspect atmosphere. Keep access clear for responders and do not crowd the boundary to watch.

At assembly, report to the designated accountability person. Tell them if someone was last seen elsewhere, including the exact location and time, without claiming the person is definitely trapped. Do not leave without being accounted for and released under the plan. A missing person triggers the planned response; it does not authorize spontaneous search teams. Reentry requires the authorized all-clear. An alarm stopping, a supervisor arriving, or equipment becoming quiet does not independently prove the hazard has ended.


### Medical first aid and rescue limits
Assess scene safety before approaching an injured person. Traffic, electricity, pressure, unstable equipment, toxic gas, fire, and confined spaces can create additional casualties. Call for trained help and use only the assistance within your training and authorization. Know where the first-aid equipment, AED, emergency shower, and eyewash are located, and keep access open. Online awareness does not supply the practical skills or certification for CPR, AED use, emergency medical care, or rescue.

For a suspected life-threatening event, activate emergency services promptly. Follow dispatcher instructions while staying within a safe scene and your ability. Do not move an injured person unnecessarily where movement could worsen injury, unless immediate danger requires a trained emergency action. Do not give food, drink, medication, or a ride to an impaired person as an improvised substitute for the medical response. Tell responders what happened, known exposures, and care already provided. Do not publicly speculate about a person's diagnosis.

A collapsed worker inside a tank, pit, vessel, or suspected hazardous atmosphere needs a planned rescue response. Do not enter, lean into the opening, or follow a second person who attempts rescue. A harness and a rope alone do not create a rescue system. Alert the designated rescue service and isolate the area from a safe position. Only trained, equipped, authorized responders use the applicable rescue plan. Many fatal events involve would-be rescuers; urgency increases the need to preserve the entry boundary.


### Bloodborne pathogens
Treat blood and designated potentially infectious materials as requiring appropriate precautions. Exposure can occur through a needlestick, cut, splash to eyes or mouth, or contact with nonintact skin. Use the employer's response arrangements and trained personnel. Appropriate gloves and other protection help prevent contact, but gloves can be punctured or transfer contamination during removal. Do not handle broken contaminated glass or sharps by hand, compress waste bags, or put a used needle into ordinary trash.

If exposure occurs, perform the relevant immediate washing or flushing, notify the designated contact promptly, and obtain urgent confidential medical evaluation through the employer's procedure. Do not use bleach on skin, squeeze a wound aggressively, or delay reporting until symptoms appear. Record the route and circumstances accurately while protecting personal information. Under 1910.1030, occupational exposure determinations drive requirements such as an exposure-control plan, training, hepatitis B vaccination offers, and post-exposure evaluation. This is not a claim that every employee has the same occupational exposure classification.


### Fire prevention and extinguisher decisions
Keep ignition sources and combustibles controlled through the work plan, including smoking locations, hot-work authorization, electrical suitability, waste storage, and bonding or grounding where required. Do not defeat a fire door, obstruct an extinguisher, or use fire equipment as ordinary storage space. Learn whether the employer requires full evacuation or permits designated workers to use extinguishers. Having an extinguisher nearby does not create a duty for every worker to fight a fire.

Only attempt an incipient-stage fire response if the employer permits it, you have the required training, the correct extinguisher is available, the alarm and emergency notification are made, and a reliable escape path remains behind you. If conditions grow, smoke impairs visibility, the fuel is unknown, a pressurized system is involved, or you doubt control, withdraw. Ordinary extinguishers cannot make an uncontrolled gas release safe. Do not extinguish a gas flame and leave an unisolated escaping fuel source without the incident command's specialist direction.

Extinguisher classes correspond to the fuel and hazard; water can be dangerous on energized electrical equipment and incompatible materials. Check the label and site training rather than relying on cylinder color. The familiar pull, aim, squeeze, sweep sequence is a memory aid, not practical qualification or a universal tactic. Inspection, maintenance, selection, and training provisions under 1910.157 depend on the employer's fire-response arrangements. Construction fire-protection provisions differ. Never delay evacuation to search for an extinguisher.


### Spills and environmental interfaces
An incidental release is one that trained personnel can safely control using the available resources without a significant emergency hazard. A spreading unknown substance, dangerous vapor, fire potential, uncontrolled source, or threat beyond local capability demands withdrawal, isolation, and the emergency plan. Do not classify a spill solely by gallons. A small release can create a dangerous atmosphere; a familiar product may still be unsafe in a poorly ventilated area.

Awareness-level workers recognize, protect themselves, notify, and keep others clear. Do not plug a leak, enter a vapor area, place absorbent, or operate a valve unless trained, equipped, authorized, and safe under the actual response procedure. HAZWOPER 1910.120 has specific scope and responder levels; this core course does not confer them. From a safe location, report product identity if known, migration direction, drains, soil or water threatened, and ignition sources. Authorized environmental personnel determine regulatory notifications and disposal. Do not wash a spill into a drain or conceal it under soil.


### Worked scenario: a collapsed tank worker
During a delivery, Elena sees a person motionless at a tank access opening. A coworker starts climbing toward them with a rope. Elena calls the established emergency contact, gives the tank identification and location, and warns the coworker to stop. She recognizes a possible atmospheric emergency, keeps others away, and moves to the safe reporting position identified by the site plan. She does not put her head through the opening to check breathing.

The trained rescue service is activated and receives the last known location and possible hazards. At muster, Elena reports both the casualty and the coworker's location so accountability is accurate. Nobody reenters because the alarm becomes quiet. Rescue and any medical assistance proceed under qualified direction. The correct outcome for an awareness worker is effective notification and prevention of additional victims, not an improvised entry.


### Worked scenario: a leak, injured hand, and approaching traffic
A forklift strikes a chemical container near a loading area. There is a sharp odor, liquid moving toward a drain, and a worker with a bleeding hand. The receiver stops nearby traffic from a safe position, sounds the alarm, and reports the container identification and drain location without walking through the liquid to read a label. Workers withdraw by the safe route, keeping clear of vapors and ignition sources.

A trained first aider attends the injured person only after reaching a safe area, using the appropriate blood-contact precautions. Any splash or blood exposure is reported for prompt evaluation. The receiver does not cover the drain personally while the atmosphere and chemical remain uncertain. Authorized responders identify the substance, control the source and migration, and arrange cleanup and environmental notifications. The event is closed only after medical follow-up, safe reentry authorization, and review of why vehicle separation failed.

### Waste prevention and fire classifications
Reduce waste at the planning stage by ordering suitable quantities, preventing contamination and choosing approved reusable equipment where compatible. Keep identified waste streams separate under the site plan; never mix materials merely to reduce container count. Mark containers, use the designated storage and disposal routes, and stop if identity or compatibility is uncertain. A drain is an environmental pathway, not a disposal instruction. Report a release promptly so the designated personnel can meet actual containment, cleanup and external-notification duties.

At recognition level, Class A concerns ordinary combustibles such as wood/paper; B concerns flammable liquids and related fuels; C indicates energized electrical involvement; D concerns combustible metals; and K concerns cooking oils/fats. Read the approved extinguisher markings and actual plan rather than choosing from color or a remembered label. The categories help explain why the wrong agent can worsen an event; they do not assign an untrained worker firefighting duties or establish compatibility with every chemical. Evacuate when the plan requires it, the conditions exceed your trained role, or escape could be lost. A trained designated user still needs the actual equipment instruction and safe practical competence.

lessons.title: Organizational safety, personal readiness, and integrated jobsite decisions
lessons.body:
## Learning objectives
- Apply employer policies without confusing policy with universal law.
- Recognize impairment, violence, stress, and short-service-worker vulnerabilities.
- Report incidents and near misses with factual, useful information.
- Integrate planning, boundaries, emergency decisions, and corrective-action verification in complete jobsite scenarios.

### Culture becomes visible in work decisions
A safety program works when workers can identify a problem, obtain help, and pause unsafe work without being pressured to hide it. Written rules matter, but scheduling, supervision, equipment availability, and responses to concerns show whether the rules can be followed. Before starting at a new employer or location, learn reporting channels, stop-work expectations, prohibited conduct, fitness requirements, emergency arrangements, and contractor coordination. Ask how to report if the immediate supervisor is involved in the concern. Do not let a missing signature or an unfamiliar reporting application delay protection from an immediate hazard.

Company requirements, client rules, manufacturer instructions, and law are different sources of obligations. An employer may set a stricter phone rule, vehicle restriction, or drug policy than a general regulation. Explain it as a policy unless an applicable legal requirement has been established. Federal OSHA general-industry and construction rules depend on the work; state-plan requirements and transportation or environmental rules may also apply. This lesson is awareness education, not legal advice, a PEC credential, or an independent authorization to perform regulated work.


### Drugs, alcohol, and work readiness
Arrive capable of performing the assigned task safely. Alcohol, illicit drugs, misuse of medication, and some properly used medications can impair coordination, attention, and judgment. Fatigue, illness, and emotional distress can create similar signs, so workers should report observed behavior rather than diagnose a coworker as intoxicated. If a person cannot safely operate equipment, stop the exposure and contact the designated supervisor or fitness resource. Do not hand them vehicle keys or tell them to drive home as a solution.

Learn the employer's possession, use, testing, disclosure, and return-to-duty policies and the procedures that apply to your role. Requirements can vary; this course does not claim a single universal testing schedule, automatic dismissal rule, or statutory waiting period after drinking. For work-relevant medication concerns, use the confidential occupational-health process and provide required functional restrictions. Do not stop prescribed treatment without medical advice or share medication with a coworker. A lawful prescription does not guarantee safe operation for every task.

A concern about fitness should produce an immediate safe work arrangement and a fair, confidential assessment. Avoid public accusations, searches, threats, or amateur sobriety tests. Document what you directly observed, such as stumbling at a ladder, delayed responses, or an admission of inadequate sleep, and when it occurred. Follow the designated process for transportation and supervision. Privacy does not mean concealing a serious immediate hazard; share necessary information with the appropriate people rather than the entire crew.


### Respectful work and violence prevention
Harassment, bullying, discriminatory behavior, threats, and intimidation undermine communication and can escalate. Treat questions and stop-work concerns respectfully, including from contractors, new workers, and workers communicating in another language. Report threatening messages, stalking, physical aggression, or coercion through the established channel. If there is immediate danger, move to safety and activate emergency help. Do not attempt to settle an escalating confrontation by blocking exits, touching the person, or matching their aggression.

For an active assailant or active-shooter event, follow the site emergency plan and responder directions. If a safe escape is available, leave the danger area, warn others when safe, and contact emergency services from safety. If escape is unsafe, use a suitable secure hiding location under the plan, reduce visibility and sound, and avoid exposing yourself to investigate. Physical resistance is a last-resort survival action when facing imminent harm, not a workplace intervention assignment. This course does not teach tactical response or authorize weapon use. Keep hands visible when encountering police and do not run toward responders carrying objects that may be misinterpreted.

Prevention includes controlled access, visitor management, clear reporting, supportive supervision, and a plan for credible threats. Do not dismiss threats as jokes because you know the speaker. Equally, avoid labeling a distressed person as violent merely because they seek mental-health support. Report specific conduct and immediate risk, not stereotypes. The responsible employer and appropriate professionals assess and respond. Save relevant messages through the approved process without circulating them as entertainment.


### Stress, mental wellbeing, and short-service workers
Stress can reduce concentration, sleep, patience, and willingness to speak up. Long shifts, uncertainty, isolation, family concerns, and repeated exposure to difficult events can accumulate. Check in respectfully when a coworker's behavior changes. Ask whether they need support, help them reach the employer's assistance resources, and adjust immediate safety-critical duties through the supervisor where needed. Do not promise secrecy when there is an immediate risk of harm. If someone expresses an immediate intent to harm themselves or others, activate emergency assistance and remain engaged only as safely appropriate; do not leave the situation to an untrained coworker.

Wellbeing support complements changes to work. Repeated overtime, poor staffing, unclear instructions, and harassment cannot be corrected solely by telling people to be resilient. Report patterns so the organization can address them. Use recovery time and available support without treating symptoms as a personal failure. Supervisors should make expectations clear and give workers realistic routes to raise concerns. This awareness lesson cannot diagnose illness or replace professional mental-health care.

A short-service worker may be new to the industry, employer, task, or location despite extensive experience elsewhere. Identify the employer's mentoring and supervision arrangements. A helmet sticker or roster designation is a communication aid, not proof of competence. The mentor should demonstrate the task, explain hazards, observe performance, and confirm understanding through teach-back. Provide language support where needed. Do not assign a new worker alone to recognize unfamiliar alarms, operate equipment, or manage permits simply because orientation is complete.

The learner also has an active role: identify limits, ask before changing methods, and report uncertainty. If the mentor is unavailable, pause tasks requiring that supervision and obtain an authorized replacement. A successful short-service period depends on demonstrated capability under the employer's process, not only elapsed days. No fixed universal mentoring duration is invented here. Every worker remains entitled and expected to raise a hazard after the introductory period ends.


### Reporting, investigation, and corrective action
Report injuries, illnesses, exposures, property damage, releases, and near misses promptly using the established channel. A near miss is useful evidence that a person reached danger without the worst outcome. First protect people and activate emergency arrangements, then preserve the scene where safe and as instructed. Do not move damaged equipment to recreate the event, delete messages, or alter a guard to make the setup look compliant. Obtain consent and follow privacy rules for photographs; never delay aid to take a picture.

Separate observation from interpretation. Record time, location, task, people present, equipment identification, conditions, what changed, existing barriers, immediate actions, and witnesses. Write that a truck moved while a worker was in the marked route rather than asserting the driver was careless without evidence. A worker's report is not the same as the employer's OSHA recordkeeping or external-reporting determination. Responsible personnel evaluate those obligations; workers should not suppress an event because they assume it is not recordable.

Effective investigations look at equipment, procedures, training, layout, communication, staffing, and organizational pressures alongside individual actions. Corrective actions need an owner, due date, interim protection, and verification of effectiveness. Telling everyone to be careful is weak if the path still crosses reversing vehicles. Verify in the actual work that the revised layout or control functions and has not created another hazard. Share applicable learning across shifts and contractors and update the task plan before repetition. Closing an electronic item without checking the field condition does not establish control.


### Integrated worked scenario: first morning on a repair crew
Noah joins a pad-maintenance crew as a short-service worker. The planned task is replacing an external bracket beside a pump, with a delivery arriving that morning. At the briefing, his mentor confirms the equipment boundary, work authorization, energy-control roles, walking route, eye and hand protection, alarm, muster, and the unloading exclusion area. Noah repeats the limits back. His mentor notices he has not used this grinder model, so a qualified worker demonstrates the setup rather than assigning independent use.

During staging, Noah sees a delivery truck begin backing while a hose blocks the pedestrian detour. He uses the agreed stop signal and stays outside the travel path. The operator stops; nobody tries to squeeze between the truck and the pump. The receiver clears and protects the walking route and reestablishes the unloading boundary. Before bracket work starts, the authorized worker verifies the specified isolation and the tool guard and accessory are checked. A delay is accepted to restore the controls.

The near miss is reported even though nobody was struck. The record identifies the obstructed detour, simultaneous delivery, briefing arrangement, and stopped movement. Investigation finds the staging plan allowed hoses in the only protected path. The corrective action moves staging and introduces a receiving check before vehicle entry, with a named owner. The next shift walks the revised route during a delivery and confirms separation works. Noah's intervention becomes a learning example without portraying him as qualified to operate the truck or isolate the pump.


### Integrated worked scenario: late shift, leak, and pressure to finish
A crew is preparing to leave after a long troubleshooting shift. Rina reports fatigue before the return drive. At the same time, a container near the work area leaks and an argument starts when someone calls the reporting worker weak. The supervisor first stops unsafe departures and separates the verbal conflict without confrontation. A relief transport arrangement is requested. Reporting fatigue is handled as useful safety information, and the disrespect concern goes through the proper channel.

The liquid is unfamiliar and moving toward a drain, so the crew activates the site response and withdraws rather than assigning the newest worker to place absorbent. From a safe position, they report container location, visible markings, migration, and nearby ignition sources. Accountability confirms everyone has moved clear. Authorized responders control the release and determine cleanup and environmental notifications. Only designated personnel approve reentry.

After immediate protection, the incident report connects the leaking container, overtime, vehicle plans, and communication breakdown without claiming they share one proven cause. Review identifies damaged storage protection and an unrealistic end-of-shift transport assumption. Actions include a protected storage arrangement, an earlier journey-fitness decision, and supervisor follow-up on respectful reporting. Each action has an owner and verification date. The job is not declared safely complete merely because the spill disappears; the crew verifies the area, restores equipment status, and completes a safe journey under the revised plan.

### Prohibited items and searches: understand the actual policy
At induction, obtain the employer and host site's rules for weapons, alcohol, drugs, unauthorized ignition sources, cameras, and other restricted items. Restrictions vary by location and applicable law; do not assume an item allowed at one facility is allowed at another. Ask how restricted items must be declared, stored, or left outside the site before bringing them through access control. Learn the written search policy, who may conduct an authorized search, what process applies, and where questions or complaints go. This lesson does not assert a universal employer right to search every person or possession, require workers to surrender legal rights, or authorize peers to search each other. If an access issue arises, stay out of the operating area and obtain the designated security or management decision without confrontation. Where a weapon or threat creates immediate danger, use emergency protective actions rather than attempting a search or seizure.

## Coverage is not workplace compliance
This register covers 68 OSHA and related applicability topics for the defined onshore knowledge scope. Each row identifies the rule or boundary, who it can affect, the course knowledge connection and what still needs evidence. No row is automatically satisfied by completing this course. An employer and qualified reviewers must determine the actual applicable rules, including state-plan additions and specialist regimes. OSHA's older training-requirements publication is an index, not a substitute for current regulations. The course cannot enumerate every possible task in every industry or complete workplace duties through a general exam.

### OSHA_01: Injury reporting and non-deterrence
Reference: 1904.35(b)(1).
Applies to: Covered employer reporting procedures.
Core connection: ESC01, ESC10. Knowledge and scenario decisions only.
Still required: Reasonable actual reporting procedure, worker information and non-retaliation practice.
Practical evidence: Not satisfied by online completion; observe/demonstrate actual skills where the cited requirement or task requires them.
Review: Employer applicability and independent review remain open.

Before assigning actual work, determine the task and jurisdiction, identify the applicable standard, document the site's procedure and hazards, provide understandable job-specific instruction, obtain the required demonstration/evaluation and records, and authorize the worker within stated limits. lessons.body:
## What is finished and what remains open
The actual lessons, worked cases, learning checks and separate VNDRLY examination are available in this course. The following external and employer duties have not been completed by authoring or publication. Every item below is OPEN. A course exam pass does not close any of them.

### IR01: Independent occupational safety reviewer
Check all 42 benchmark mappings against actual lesson paragraphs, scenarios and assessment coverage, document omissions and resolve them before any external equivalence claim.
Status: OPEN.

### IR02: Qualified regulatory reviewers for actual industry/jurisdiction
Validate applicability, current federal/state requirements and task exclusions in every OSHA row; review actual employer/site evidence. This is an author-prepared coverage register, not a compliance determination.
Status: OPEN.

### IR03: Assessment specialist independent of course sales
Job/knowledge analysis, examination blueprint and item review, defensible passing standard, accessibility/fairness, item statistics, retest exposure and retention study. Current 80% threshold is provisional VNDRLY policy.
Status: OPEN.

### IR04: Qualified instructors and learner pilot reviewers
Evaluate teaching accuracy, comprehension, learner duration, accessibility and delivery. Self-paced publication is not evidence of eight instructional hours or equivalence to instructor-led delivery.
Status: OPEN.

### IR05: VNDRLY credential governance and independent auditor
Validate identity assurance/proctoring, security, privacy, records, complaints/appeals, conflicts of interest, version changes, suspension/revocation and any chosen accreditation route. Current exam is account-authenticated, not independently proctored.
Status: OPEN.

### IR06: Each accepting partner/operator

External application, curriculum/delivery/instructor audits and formal approval. Published objective coverage does not grant accreditation or permission to issue another organization’s credential.

## Record a defensible practical evaluation
Identify the worker; task, equipment and method; the applicable safe arrangement; assessor identity and competence basis; observed criteria; actual results and any failed criteria; date; restrictions and corrective instruction; reassessment triggers; and the responsible employer's authorization decision. Do not mark physical performance observed because a learner answered an online question or acknowledged a displayed correction.

## Partner acceptance
Until the accepting partner records written approval for this exact version and delivery, treat the credential as VNDRLY internal knowledge evidence. A partner's general wording allowing an equivalent course is an invitation to evaluate evidence, not an approval of this course. Retain required third-party credentials when a contract or site still requires them. No partner acceptance, accreditation or practical observation is manufactured by the course.
